New Temporary & Permanent Course Email

The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:

Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.

Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

lines: Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "method of instruction.”
Instructional Delivery Method

Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.
# Lecture
A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
# Laboratory
Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
# Recitation
Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
# Studio
Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
# Seminar
Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
# Independent Study

One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
# Practicum
Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
# Workshop
Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.

pages.title: Choosing the Right Proposal Type
lines: Choosing the Right Proposal Type
Course Proposal Types

There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. Selecting the correct proposal type is important. Proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
Course modifications that are sometimes mistaken for new courses include:
Making a temporary course permanent
Changing the subject code of an existing course
Adding a new cross-listing to an existing course
A new course proposal is appropriate for:
Creating a new permanent course
Creating a new temporary course
Program Proposal Types

There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct proposal type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
# Program Credential Types

In addition to selecting the appropriate proposal type, each program is classified under one of four credential types: Degree, Major, Certificate, or Minor. The credential type identifies the type of academic program being proposed.
Degree
An academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of a prescribed program of study. Degrees include bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees.

In Kuali, select Degree when the program is the only program offered under that degree. Examples include the MPS (Master of Professional Studies), BIS (Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies), Pharm.D. (Doctor of Pharmacy), and DNP (Doctor of Nursing Practice).
Major
A defined field of study within a degree program consisting of a required set of courses and related academic requirements in a specific discipline.
In Kuali, select Major when the program is one of multiple options offered under the same degree. These typically include BA, BS, MA, MS, and PhD programs.
Certificate
A formal program of study consisting of a defined set of courses in a focused area. Certificates may be completed independently or in conjunction with a degree program.
Minor
A secondary field of study consisting of a prescribed set of courses in a discipline outside a student’s major. A minor is intended to complement a student’s primary area of study.
Specialization Proposal Types

There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct proposal type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
# 🚨 Understanding Specializations, Sub-Plans, Options, Tracks, Focus Areas, and Concentrations
At URI, these terms refer to different curricular structures. Understanding how they differ is essential to ensure that programs and their areas of study are proposed and documented correctly.
# Specializations, Sub-Plans, Options, and Tracks
These represent a formally recognized area of study within a program. They:
Are coded in eCampus
Have defined requirements that students must complete
Appear on the student’s transcript
Are formally created and maintained through the Specializations section of Kuali
Note: The terminology used may vary by system or University Manual terminology. For curricular proposal purposes, these structures are treated as specializations in Kuali.
# Concentrations and Focus Areas
These represent an optional area of study within a program. They:
Are not coded in eCampus
May include suggested courses or course sequences to guide students
Do not appear on the student’s transcript
Are described within the program description to which they belong
Do not require a separate curricular proposal
# What about ABMs and “4 + 1” Programs?

Both Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s (ABM) programs and “4 + 1” programs are formally recognized Specializations, but they differ in how they are structured and which degree program they belong to.
ABM Specializations
Are inherited by the Master’s degree
Identify a defined pathway from the Bachelor’s degree into the Master’s degree
Include an identified set of courses that may be double-counted toward both the Bachelor’s and Master’s degree requirements
“4 + 1” Specializations
Are inherited by the Bachelor’s degree
Do not include courses that are double-counted toward both degrees
Provide guidance on courses students should take during the final semesters of their undergraduate degree to help shorten the time needed to complete the Master’s degree

lines: Tags: programs
Short Description: The University Catalog description of an academic program, including its curriculum, degree requirements, and other requirements for completion.
Program Description

The University Catalog description of the requirements for completing an academic program, including the courses and credits required for the major, General Education, and free electives, as well as any additional program-specific requirements.
# Description Formatting for the Catalog/Kuali
# Degree and Major Description Formatting
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose of the program and the significance of the degree or major.
Specializations: The specializations (sub-plans) should be listed by name, but the requirements should not be listed in the program description.
Major Requirements: Listed, required courses
Professional Electives: Students choose from a list of courses selected specifically to align with the content of the program
Free Electives: Students are free to choose. Must provide a credit amount, minimum 6 credits for undergraduate degrees are required
Cumulative GPA and/or major GPA requirements
“A minimum GPA of 2.0 is required for graduation”
Total number of credits required to graduate
“A minimum of 120 credits is required for graduation”
Other Common Statements
“At least XX of all required courses for graduation must be numbered 300 and above”
“Students must earn a grade of X or better in all required courses”
“Students must complete a minimum of XX credits in the major”
“At least XX credits must be completed at the 300-level or above”
Total number of credits required to graduate (use the following phrase)
“A minimum of 120 credits is required for graduation”
# Minor Description Formatting
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose and significance of the minor.
Course Requirements
# Certificate Description Formatting
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose and significance of the certificate.
Course Requirements
Total number of credits required to graduate
# Requirements
# Degree or Major Program Requirements
An undergraduate student’s field of study is called the “major” (UM 8.20.40)
A graduate student’s field of study is called the “program” (UM 8.20.40)
Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)
# Minor Requirements
18 or more credits of related studies offered by one or more departments or programs and sponsored by a faculty member. (UM 8.20.50)
At least 12 credits at the 200-level or above ( UM 8.20.51)
At least 8 credits must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.51)
Minimum GPA average of 2.0 must be earned in the minor’s required courses (UM 8.20.51)
A maximum of two courses can apply to both the major and minor field of study (UM 8.20.52)
# Certificate Requirements
Undergraduate certificates generally require 15-21 credits of coursework (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificates are available to degree seeking and certificate-only seeking undergraduate students (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificate courses may not be pass/fail (UM 8.20.71)
Graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 16 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)
Post-master’s graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 18 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)

lines: Tags: courses
Short Description: The numerical portion of a course identifier that follows the Subject Code (e.g., ENG101, where ENG is the Subject Code and 101 is the Course Number).
Course Number

Pre-freshman and special undergraduate. Characteristics: Undergraduate courses not applicable for degree credit. Post-Secondary or sub-freshman remedial courses, Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies courses for no credit or for non-credit certificate credit only.

Lower division undergraduate courses. Primarily for freshmen and sophomores and as electives for upper class students. Characteristics: Little or no prior college level work required. May not be taken for graduate credit.

Upper division undergraduate courses. Primarily for juniors and seniors majoring in the field or advanced students in other disciplines. Characteristics: Some formal background or sophistication required but not to the extent that would ordinarily justify allowing graduate degree credit.

Generally limited to juniors and seniors majoring in the field. Open to other advanced undergraduates and to graduate students with permission. Characteristics: Extensive background required, may be taken for graduate credit. (Limitations may be stated by the department if desired.)
Courses numbered at the 400 level that are available for graduate credit must be approved by both the appropriate Undergraduate Curriculum Committee (CASC or GEC) and the Graduate Council.

Graduate level courses. The bachelor’s degree is usually a prerequisite but qualified seniors and honors students can be admitted with permission. Characteristics: Comprise majority of course work between bachelor’s and master’s degree. Number 599 reserved for masters thesis research and is graded on an S/U-only basis.

Advanced graduate courses. No undergraduates admitted except honors students with approval of advisors and the department. Characteristics: Comprise majority of course work between master’s and doctor’s degree but not limited to doctoral students. Number 699 reserved for doctoral thesis research and is graded on an S/U-only basis.

Special types of graduate courses for which no program credit is allowed. Characteristics: Workshops, institutes, courses taken for certificate credit only, courses taken to remedy deficiencies, and temporary courses which have not been approved by the Graduate Council for graduate program credit.

pages.title: Credential Type
lines: Tags: programs

Short Description: Identifies the type of academic credential awarded for a program. 
(Degree, Major, Minor, Certificate)
Credential Type
# Degrees & Majors

The degree is the academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of an approved program of study and its associated requirements. Degrees may include bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees.
The major is the primary field of study within a degree program, consisting of a defined set of courses and requirements that students must complete.

University Manual 8.20.40 Major Fields of Study. An undergraduate student’s concentrated field of study in a degree-granting college shall be the student’s “major”; Fannon Institute students may have a “preferred major.” The major field of study for graduate students shall be the student’s “program.”
# Degree / Major Program Requirements
Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)
In Kuali, the term program refers to all credential types; Degrees, majors, minors, and certificates. In the Manual, program refers to a graduate student’s major field of study.
# Minor

A secondary concentration of undergraduate courses that provides students with a defined area of study outside their major. A minor generally requires 18 or more credits and is listed on the student’s permanent academic record after graduation.
University Manual 8.20.50 Minor Fields of Study. Undergraduate Students may declare a “minor” field of study. A minor is a secondary concentration of courses.
# Minor Requirements
18 or more credits of related studies offered by one or more departments or programs and sponsored by a faculty member. (UM 8.20.50)
At least 12 credits at the 200-level or above ( UM 8.20.51)
At least 8 credits must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.51)
Minimum GPA average of 2.0 must be earned in the minor’s required courses (UM 8.20.51)
A maximum of two courses can apply to both the major and minor field of study (UM 8.20.52)
# Certificate
An approved course of study designed to further knowledge in a field of interest, provide specialized training, and/or enhance professional skills.
# Certificate Requirements
Undergraduate certificates generally require 15-21 credits of coursework (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificates are available to degree seeking and certificate-only seeking undergraduate students (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificate courses may not be pass/fail (UM 8.20.71)
Graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 16 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)
Post-master’s graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 18 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)

A. Build knowledge of diverse peoples and cultures and of the natural and physical world.

C. Exercise individual and social responsibilities.

D. Integrate and apply these abilities and capacities, adapting them to new settings, questions, and responsibilities to lay the foundation for lifelong learning.

pages.title: Temporary Course
lines: Tags: courses
Short Description: A course approved for limited offerings, typically to test an experimental course or address a temporary need. Also known as an “X-Course.”
Temporary Course

UM 8.80.12 A temporary course may be offered no more than twice and only during a two-year period following its approval. A temporary course must meet one or more of the following criteria: a) it is experimental in nature. It is innovative, using unconventional devices or pedagogical methods, course materials, approach to course content or student-teacher relationships; b) it is being tried out on a temporary basis so that its value and effectiveness can be tested before it is added to a department’s permanent curriculum; c) it is intended for a limited duration, such as in the case of employing a visiting specialist temporarily available or to satisfy temporary needs and interests of students or to deal with timely issues.

UM 8.81.30 A Temporary Course shall have approval of the department(s) or committee proposing it, the dean(s) of the college(s) involved, and the Curriculum and Standards Committee and/or the Graduate Council, except that a temporary University College mini-course (a one-credit lower-level undergraduate course taught during the fall or spring semester) does not require the approval of the Curriculum and Standards Committee. The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall, however, receive information about any temporary University College mini-course after it has been approved by the college dean. The Graduate Council may refuse to grant or may attach conditions to the granting of graduate program credit for a temporary course. Each college may require internal channels of approval in addition to those specified here.

UM 8.81.31 The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the Graduate Council shall give priority at their meetings to the consideration of proposed temporary courses. Prior to approving temporary courses, these committees shall distribute to all faculty a description of these courses and shall provide faculty members with a seven-day period in which to register comments with the Chairperson of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and/or with the Dean of the Graduate School.

UM 8.81.60 It is the responsibility of the Office of Enrollment Services to limit the offering of a temporary course to only twice during a two-year period and to limit to three times the offering of a specific topic within an open-ended course.

lines: Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
How to input Courses Approved for Double Counting in your ABM Specialization form.
Whether you are creating a new ABM, or modifying an existing, you will be asked to input all courses approved for double counting in a “Rules” gadget.
# Adding Double-Counted Courses
Click Use Rule Categories checkbox
Click + Add Rules
In the blank box next to A, click the drop-down carrot, and select Double-Count.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select minimum number of credits from.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select selected courses.
Enter the total number of double-counted course credits in the Credits box. In the Courses box, list all courses that may be used toward these credits.
If the ABM allows only a certain number of credits from the courses specified, you can end here and move on to the next section of your form.
# Adding Approved Course Statements

If you would like to add a statement indicating that other courses may be considered for double-counting with input from an advisor, program director, or other appropriate individual, follow these steps:
Click the plus (+) sign underneath the blue Update Logic button.
You will now see a blank box labeled with the letter B. In this box, click the drop-down carrot, and select Free form text.
Enter the text to accompany the courses selected.
Text Examples:
“Other 400-level ENG courses approved for graduate credit may be chosen in consultation with the program director.”
“Any 500-level CSF course approved by the advisor.”
“Nine credits may be double counted for the ABM Degree. Only 500­-level courses and 400­-level courses designated for graduate credit are eligible to be double counted.”

Undergraduate: A program leading to an undergraduate degree or credential, such as a bachelor’s degree, undergraduate certificate, or minor.

lines: Tags: courses

Short Description: A roadmap for a course that communicates its scope, learning outcomes, expectations, policies, assessments, and other essential information students need to successfully complete the course.
Syllabus

University Manual 8.50.30 Course Syllabi. All instructors shall make available a syllabus in the first week of class, or first day of class for fully-online accelerated programs (8.51.24), to students enrolled in each of their courses.  Syllabi components should clearly communicate classroom policies, essential aspects of the course, and expectations of student participation.

University Manual 8.51.24 For online courses taught in the fully-online accelerated calendar, final projects and/or final exams shall be scheduled by faculty according to the learning outcomes of the class and best pedagogical practices for online learning. The calendar of due dates for assignments and assessments shall be in the syllabus and available to students on the first day of class. No final exam or final project shall be due after the last day of the session.
From the Provost:

In addition to satisfying Faculty Senate approved policies, your syllabus communicates mutual expectations between you and your students and serves as a roadmap to successful course completion, including your course scope, expectations, learning outcomes, deadlines, attendance policies, grading criteria, and other important information. Please provide students with information about assessment/major paper/project due dates, office hours, availability of special tutorial sessions, and expectations on individual vs group work. This clear outlining of expectations helps to ensure that students in your classes understand what they are expected to learn, how they will be assessed, and are fully aware of your academic standards. Providing such information can help avoid misunderstanding, frustration—on both sides—and foster acceptance of responsibility by our students

Topics courses allow different topics to be offered under the same course number.

8.81.20  Open-ended Course. An Open-ended Course shall be administered by the department which originated it. Initially, an open-ended course shall be proposed and approved in the same manner as other permanent courses (8.81.10). Prior to offering a specific topic the content of the course shall be approved in a department meeting.

8.81.21 After approval of each offering of an open-ended course topic, a copy of the title, subtitle, and description shall be forwarded for schedule authorization to the Office of Enrollment Services via the dean of the college in which the department resides. The dean’s authorization shall ensure that no overlap exists between specific topics and existing courses.

8.81.22 A specific topic within an open-ended course may be offered three times. After three offerings the topic shall be approved through the appropriate channels as either a permanent course or as a permanent topic within an open-ended course and shall be included in the University Catalog.

pages.title: Track Your Proposal
lines: Track Your Proposal
Quick Links

Submitting a curricular proposal in Kuali begins a structured, multi-level review process, and we know you’re eager to know when your item will be reviewed and approved. While timelines vary across colleges, this guide will help you understand where your proposal is in the process and when to expect its full approval.
# The Quick Version
For those who already know how the process works, but simply need directions on where to find the status:
Open the proposal in Kuali
Expand the workflow status
# Step-by-Step Guide
# Step 1: Understand the approval path
All curricular proposals move through multiple levels of review. While this can vary slightly, most proposals follow this sequence:
Department-level review(s)
College Curriculum Committee
College Dean
Faculty Senate Curriculum Committees (Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards, General Education)
Faculty Senate (courses are fully approved at this level)
University President (program modifications and new certificates, minors, and specializations are approved at this level)
Board of Trustees (new major and degree programs are approved at this level)
Each step depends on the successful approval at the previous level.
Check out The Approval Process for a flowchart and more detailed explanation of the approval process.
# The Approval Process
# Step 2: Know the current proposal status
All who have access to Kuali have the ability to check on the status of every proposal currently under review. To find the current workflow status:
Open the proposal in Kuali.
Access it from your dashboard if you are the proposer, or
Search for it in the Proposals section, and use filters to refine results
Review the workflow status. At the top of the proposal page, the workflow status shows:
The current stage of approval
The users in the role of approving that step
Expand for full details. Clik the expand option to the right of “Workflow Status” to view:
The completed approval steps, and
The remaining steps before final approval.
# Step 3: Know the submission deadlines

Department, college, and Faculty Senate committees each have deadlines for including proposals on their meeting agendas. Faculty should consult with their department or college curriculum committees for specific deadlines at those levels of approval.
Each summer, submission deadlines are set for college deans to help ensure proposals are approved by the Faculty Senate on a predictable timeline.

Curriculum proposals must receive all required approvals by specific deadlines to take effect for their intended term. Deadlines vary by proposal type and may be influenced by registration dates, implementation requirements, and additional University approvals.

Unless otherwise noted, this does not apply to graduate proposals.
# Step 4: Factor in Revisions
Many proposals require revisions during the review process. The following meeting results can impact your approval timeline:
Tabled: The committee needs additional information before making a decision. Once the requested information is provided, the proposal will be reviewed again at the next meeting.

Contingently Approved: The proposal is approved pending minor revisions or clarifications. No additional committee review is required. Once the conditions are met, the proposal will move to the next step.
Sent Back: The proposal requires substantial revisions. It must be updated and resubmitted, at which point it will re-enter the workflow from the beginning.
# Step 5: Track Your Proposal Status
Proposal statuses can be tracked by logging into Kuali and expanding the workflow, or by searching for items that have been fully approved by the college in the proposal tracker.
2026-2027 Proposal Tracker

Please note: The proposal tracker is updated manually by the Faculty Senate Office and is not automated. While every effort is made to ensure accuracy, occasional errors may occur and are typically corrected after each Faculty Senate meeting. For the most up-to-date status, please check Kuali.
# Step 6: Final Check
By the Monday prior to each monthly Faculty Senate meeting, the Faculty Senate Office distributes the Senate agenda to all faculty.
This agenda includes reports from the Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards Committee, and General Education Committee, which are voted on during the meeting.

If your proposal has been approved by a committee but does not appear on the agenda, please contact the committee chair or the Faculty Senate Office. Reports are prepared manually, and with a high volume of proposals each month, occasional errors may occur. These are typically resolved quickly.
# Course Proposals after the Senate Meeting

The integration between Kuali and PeopleSoft is not immediate, can take several days, and requires review by Enrollment Services to ensure all information migrated accurately. Please allow up to two weeks after the Senate Meeting for new courses and course modifications to appear in eCampus.
# Program Proposals after the Senate Meeting

Once curriculum committee reports are approved by the Faculty Senate, they are converted into Bills. Bills are signed by the Faculty Senate President and forwarded to the University President for review and signature. Once the University President signs & approves, the Bills are returned to the Faculty Senate Office and the proposals are approved in Kuali.
Special Case: New Majors and New Degree Programs

After University President approval, these proposals are forwarded to the Board of Trustees. Once the Faculty Senate Office confirms Board approval, the new major or degree is fully approved in Kuali.

Content Overlap

Proposed courses, programs, and specializations are reviewed for potential content overlap with existing curricula. Proposers should review existing curricula and ensure that proposed courses, programs, and specializations do not contain substantial actual or perceived content overlap.
Early consultation with potentially affected academic units may help identify concerns, clarify distinctions between offerings, and support an efficient review process.

A letter of support, which may be provided as an email from an affected department chair, can be uploaded to the Kuali proposal to document (a) that both departments have considered potential content overlap; (b) communication between the affected department and the department proposing the curriculum; and (c) the affected department’s support for the proposed curriculum.

# The Approval Process

The curriculum approval process generally follows the sequence shown in the URI Curricular Approval Process Flowchart. Specific steps may vary by college, department, proposal type, and whether the proposal requires additional levels of review.
URI Curricular Approval Process Flowchart
# Overview

Proposal Development
Faculty use the forms in Kuali Curriculum Management to develop the proposal and work with other stakeholders as appropriate.

Department Review
The proposal is reviewed through the appropriate departmental process.

College Curriculum Committee Review
The College Curriculum Committee reviews the proposal.

College Dean Approval
The College Dean approves the proposal for Faculty Senate review.

Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee Review
The Curriculum & Standards Committee, the General Education Committee, or the Graduate Council reviews the proposal.

Faculty Senate Approval
The Faculty Senate considers the curriculum committee's recommendation and votes.

University President Approval
Any curricular item that is not a course must be reviewed and approved by the University President.

URI Board of Trustees Approval
In addition to the University President’s approval, new Majors and Degrees are also reviewed by the Board of Trustees.

# What is an approval round?
An approval round is the sequence of review and approval activities that culminates in a Faculty Senate meeting. Multiple approval rounds occur throughout the academic year, and rounds may overlap.

Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. lines: Course Modification Proposal Walkthrough

This guide provides step-by-step procedural instructions for completing and submitting a Course Modification Proposal in Kuali. It focuses on navigating the form, including what to select or enter in each field.
The guide is organized by proposal section (panel), so you can jump directly to a section when you need help.
This guide does not provide guidance on course content or academic decisions. Consult your department and applicable curriculum committees for questions about developing the course itself.
Related toolkit entry: Specialization Modification Proposal Walkthrough
# Before you begin
# Understand URI’s Curricular Process

Familiarize yourself with URI’s curricular process before beginning your proposal. This will help you understand the steps involved in the curricular process and accurately estimate how long your proposal may take to reach approval.
How the Curriculum Process Works
Related toolkit entry: How the Curriculum Process Works
Approval Calendar
Related toolkit entry: Approval Calendar
# Make Sure You Can Access Kuali CM
You will need access to Kuali Curriculum Management (Kuali CM) to propose any curricular item.
Kuali Basics
Related toolkit entry: Kuali Basics
# Choose the Right Proposal Type
Some course proposal types can be easily confused. If you are unsure which type applies, review these common examples.
Table columns: If you want to… | Use…
If you want to…: Make a Temporary Course a Permanent Course which appears in the Academic Catalog | Use…: Course Modification Proposal
If you want to…: Create a new cross-listing to accompany an existing course | Use…: Course Modification Proposal

If you want to…: Add a new topic to an open-ended topics course | Use…: New Course Proposal if the course is a GCH course

No proposal needed for any other subject code. Contact Enrollment Services to add the new topic.
If you want to…: Add a new topic to a permanent topics course | Use…: Course Modification Proposal
If you want to…: Create a new 500-level section of a course to accompany the 400-level | Use…: New Course Proposal
# Start the Proposal
From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).
Select Curriculum to open your Dashboard .
Related toolkit entry: Dashboard
From the left-hand navigation menu, select Courses.
On the Courses page, use the search bar at the top to find the course you would like to modify. You can search by:
Course code (e.g., COM100)
Course title (e.g., Communication Fundamentals)
Keywords found in the course title, description, or anywhere in the course form.
Once you locate the course, select it to open the current version
With the current course open, select Propose Changes in the upper-right corner of the window.
A window will appear prompting you to select Create a new version or Create a new revision. Always select Create a new version.
The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.
# Course Modification Proposal
This is where you will indicate the changes you are proposing to make to the course.

Select the type(s) of change: Check Major, Minor, or both, depending on the changes you are proposing. 
If you’re not sure which category applies, that’s okay! Select an option to view the list of changes included in that category.
Select the specific change(s): From the list(s) that appear, check the box next to each Major and/or Minor change you are proposing.
# Major Changes
# Change the course description

Modify the description of a course. For example: Introduces students to the principles of environmental sustainability, with emphasis on climate change, resource management, and sustainable practices and their applications in modern society.
See Course Description
Related toolkit entry: Course Description
# Add or change a modality

Add: Add a new modality to a course (e.g., add an in-person option to an online course).
Change: Change the modality in which a course is offered (e.g., change an in-person course to online).
See Modality
Related toolkit entry: Modality
# Change the method of instruction
Change the method of instruction for a course (e.g., Lecture to Seminar or Lecture to Lecture and Recitation).
See Method of Instruction
Related toolkit entry: Method of Instruction
# Change the course number to a new hundred level
Change a course number to a different hundred level (e.g., BIO318 to BIO418).
See Course Number
Related toolkit entry: Course Number
# Add new general education outcomes

Add GE outcomes to a course that does not currently have any, or add a new GE outcome to a course that already has been approved for GE (this may involve replacing an existing outcome, or adding a second outcome to a course currently approved for only one).
See General Education Outcomes
Related toolkit entry: General Education Outcomes
# Add new topic to GCH course
Because GCH courses carry General Education outcomes, each new topic must be reviewed by the General Education Committee.
See GCH Topics
Related toolkit entry: GCH Topics
# Change the grading method of a GE course
All GE outcomes must have a grading method of Letter Grades, with the exception of D1 which can also be graded as S/U. Therefore, this only applies to D1 courses.
See Grading Method
Related toolkit entry: Grading Method
# Change number of fixed credits
Change the number of fixed credits for a course (e.g., 3 to 4 credits).
See Credits.
Related toolkit entry: Credits
# Change fixed credits to a credit range
Change a course with fixed credits (e.g., 3 credits) to a credit range (e.g., 3–4 credits or 1–3 credits).
See Credits
# Change the credit range outside of current range
Change a course’s credit range from 3–6 credits to a range that falls outside of 3–6 credits (e.g., 1–6, 3–12, or 1–12).
See Credits
# Change varied credits to a fixed credit outside of current range
Change a course with a credit range (e.g., 3–6 credits) to a fixed number of credits outside the current range (e.g., 2 credits or 7 credits).
See Credits
# Add graduate credit to a 400-level course
Allow a 400-level course to count for graduate credit, either as an elective in a graduate program or for double counting in an ABM program.
# Minor Changes
# Delete course
Remove the course from the University’s course offerings, the catalog, and inactivate it in eCampus.
# Change course title
Introduction to Digital Media and Design Fundamentals
SeeCourse Title
Related toolkit entry: Course Title
# Change academic home (department / college)
Move a course from one department or college to another.
# Remove a modality
Remove one of the modalities in which a course is currently offered, so that the course is offered in only one modality (in-person / online)
See Modality
# Change prerequisites
Add, remove, or change a course prerequisite.
# Change subject code
Change the subject code assigned to a course, such as changing BIO to CMB.
# Add a cross-listing

Add a new cross-listed subject code to a course. For example:
MBA545 becomes MBA545(BUS545), or 
MBA543(BUS543) adds FIN543, becoming MBA543 (BUS543, FIN543).
SeeCross-listed Course
Related toolkit entry: Cross-listed Course
# Remove a cross-listing

Remove an existing cross-listed subject code from a course. For example:
MBA543(BUS543, FIN543) becomes MBA543(BUS543).
SeeCross-listed Course
# Remove general education outcomes
Remove one or more general education outcomes from a course.
# Change temporary course to permanent
Make a temporary course permanent so that it can continue to be offered beyond the two times permitted within the two years after approval.
See Temporary Course
Related toolkit entry: Temporary Course
# Change open ended topic course type (permanent topics vs. temporary topics)
Change whether an open-ended course is offered with permanent topics or temporary topics. Permanent topics are listed in the course description, while temporary topics are not.
See Topics Course
Related toolkit entry: Topics Course
# Change grading method of a non-GE course
Change whether a non-General Education course is graded using letter grades, S/U grading, or both.
See Grading Method
# Change course number within the hundred level
Change a course number while keeping it within the same hundred level (e.g., BIO101 to BIO105).
# Change credit range inside of the current range
Narrow a course’s credit range without changing its existing minimum or maximum credits (e.g., 1–6 credits to 2–5 credits).
See Credits
# Change varied credits to fixed credits within current range
Change a course with a credit range to a fixed number of credits that falls within the current range (e.g., 3–6 credits to 4 credits).
See Credits
# Change course repeat criteria
Change the conditions under which a course may be repeated for credit.
See Repeat Criteria
Related toolkit entry: Repeat Criteria
# Remove graduate credit from a 400-level course
Remove the option for a 400-level course to count for graduate credit.

Rationale
Briefly describe the rationale for the proposed changes.
🔽 The following field will appear only if a syllabus is required based on the checkboxes selected above.

Syllabus
Upload the course syllabus here.
# Contact Information
Complete the following fields with your contact information.

Proposer Name
Your name is automatically populated based on your Kuali account.

Proposer Title
Enter your university role.

Proposer Email
Enter your URI email address. This is the email reviewers will use if they have questions about your proposal.
# Course Administration

Effective Term & Year
Select the term and year in which you intend the course to become effective. If the effective term entered at proposal submission has missed the deadline by the time it reaches the Faculty Senate, this field will be automatically updated to the next available semester.

Academic Career
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless one of the following applies:
The course number or level is changing. For example, an undergraduate-level course is becoming a graduate-level course, or vice versa.
The course is moving from the Traditional Calendar to the Accelerated Online Calendar, or vice versa.
Changing the Academic Calendar?

Good to know: If a course is already approved for online instruction, you do not need a proposal to offer it in the other academic calendar, as long as it will remain online. You can simply contact Enrollment Services to schedule the course in the other calendar.
A proposal is required when the change also involves a change in modality (for example, changing from online to in-person).
Which situation applies to you?
# Adding an Accelerated Online (7-week) section of a course already approved for online instruction?
No proposal is needed as long as there are no other changes to the course. Contact Enrollment Services to schedule the course in the Accelerated Online Calendar.
# Adding a Traditional (14-week) online section of a course already approved for online instruction in the Accelerated Online Calendar?
No proposal is needed as long as there are no other changes to the course. Contact Enrollment Services to schedule the course in the Traditional Calendar.
# Adding an Accelerated Online (7-week) section of a course currently approved only for in-person instruction?

A proposal is required because you are adding a new modality. On the proposal, keep the original 14-week calendar radio button selected under Academic Calendar. In your rationale, explain that you intend to continue offering the course in the Traditional Calendar while also adding an online section to the Accelerated Online Calendar.
Example: “We want to continue to offer this course in the Traditional Calendar, as well as add an online section to the Accelerated Online Calendar.”
# Adding an in-person section to a course currently approved only for the Accelerated Online (7-week) Calendar?

A proposal is required because you are adding a new modality. On the proposal, keep the original 7-week accelerated calendar radio button selected under Academic Calendar. In your rationale, explain that you intend to continue offering the course in the Accelerated Online Calendar while also adding an in-person section to the Traditional Calendar.
Example: “We want to continue to offer this course in the Accelerated Online Calendar, as well as add an in-person section to the Traditional Calendar.”

College
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change academic home (department/college) in the first section of the form.

Department
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change academic home (department/college) in the first section of the form.
🔽 The following field will appear only if Change academic home was checked.

Letter(s) of support from outgoing department / college.
Upload confirmation from the original department/college that they are in support of the course moving to a new academic home.

Honors Program
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is.
🔽 The following field will appear only if  “Yes” is chosen for Honors Program.

Honors Type
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is.

General Education
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add new general education outcomes (and the course was not GE previously), or Remove general education outcomes in the first section of the form.
# Course Information

Subject Code
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change subject code in the first section of the form.
Remember: The subject code must be owned by the College and Department previously entered in the form.

Number
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change course number within the hundred level or Change course number to a new hundred level in the first section of the form. A few reminders:
The course numbering system is found in UM 8.30.10.
Temporary course numbers end with an “X”
Grand Challenge course numbers end with a “G”

Is this a 400-level course available for graduate credit?
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add graduate credit to a 400-level course or Remove graduate from a 400-level course in the first section of the form.

Course Title
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change course title in the first section of the form.

Abbreviated Course Title
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change course title in the first section of the form.

Course Description
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you are changing the course description, the general education outcomes, the grading method, the repeat criteria, the credits or credit range, removing or adding 400-level for graduate credit, the prerequisites, the cross-listing(s), or the repeat criteria. (Click on the Course Description link for more information).

Supporting Materials
Optional. Use this file upload to provide additional information that may be helpful to review committees before the proposal enters the approval workflow.
# Modality, Method of Instruction, and Prerequisites

Modality
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add or change a modality in the first section of the form.

Method of Instruction
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change the method of instruction in the first section of the form.
Note that “Online” is not a method of instruction; it was removed from the list of methods of instruction in 2025. If this still remains entered in your proposal, please change it.
If the course has multiple methods of instruction, select the first as Primary and all additional methods as Secondary.
If the course has two or more methods of instruction, indicate how the methods are divided. This information is important for Enrollment Services; omitting it may delay final approval.

Requisites
Confirm the prerequisites in this textbox. Copy them exactly as they are listed in the description unless you have checked Change prerequisites in the first section of the form.
# Cross-listed Courses

Is this a cross-listed course?
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add a cross-listing or Remove a cross-listing in the first section of the form.
🔽 The following fields will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Is this a cross-listed course?

Cross-listed course(s) for eCampus
Make sure all cross-listed courses are entered (existing and proposed)

Cross-listed course(s) for the Catalog
Make sure all cross-listed courses are entered here as well (existing and proposed).

Cross-listed Department(s)
Make sure all departments are entered here which belong to the cross-listed courses (existing and proposed).

Letter(s) of support from cross-listed departments
For new courses and course modifications, the “parent” department (the department associated with the course code on the proposal) must provide a letter of support from each cross-listed department.
🔽 The following fields will appear only if Remove a cross-listing is checked in the first section of the form.

Letter(s) of support from removed cross-listed department(s)
Upload confirmation and support from the department of the proposed removed cross-listed course.
What if my cross-listed course code belongs to the same department as the parent course code? For example, MCE and ISE are both in the Department of Mechanical, Industrial & Systems Engineering.
Just upload a document stating: “Both subject codes belong to the same department.”
# Grading Method, Credits, and Repeat Criteria

Credits
This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked one of the following in the first section of the form:
Change number of fixed credits
Change fixed credits to a credit range
Change the credit range outside of current range
Change varied credits to a fixed credit outside of current range
Change credit range inside of the current range
Change varied credits to fixed credits within current range

Grading Method
Select letter grades, S/U, or both.

Can this course be repeated for credit?
Select Yes or No.
🔽 The following fields will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Can this course be repeated for credit?

Maximum times course may be taken:
Enter max number of times.

Maximum credits allowed:
Enter the maximum number of credits a student may earn for the course. For example, a 3-credit course that may be taken three times for credit has a maximum of 9 credits.

Can students repeat within the same term?
Select Yes or No.
🔽 The following field will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Can students repeat within the same term?

Maximum credits allowed per term:
Enter the maximum number of credits a student may earn from this course within a single term.
# General Education Outcomes
🔽 This section will appear only if  Yes is chosen from General Education.
If this course is already approved for general education, the following fields will already be populated.
Proposers do not need to fill out the outcome tables for outcomes already approved. However, tables for new outcomes need to be filled out according to the requirements.

Learning Outcome 1
Select the appropriate learning outcome from the dropdown and complete the table for your first outcome.

Learning Outcome 2
Courses must have at least one General Education learning outcome and may have up to two. Based on your selection for Learning Outcome 1, the applicable options will be available in this dropdown. If you are not adding a second outcome, leave this field blank.
If selected, complete the table for your second outcome.

Is this a grand challenge?
Select Yes or No.
# Grand Challenge
🔽 This section will appear only if the course is for general education credit, and if Yes is chosen for Is this a grand challenge?

If this course is already approved for the Grand Challenge, you do not need to complete the following fields. Because Grand Challenge courses were established before Kuali, some fields may not have existing information. If you are required to enter something in a text field in order to submit the proposal to workflow, you may enter “—”.
GRAND CHALLENGE: Explain how the course title, syllabus, and assignments demonstrate the contemporary challenge addressed by the course.

INTERDISCIPLINARY: Explain how the course incorporates at least two disciplinary perspectives and provides opportunities for students to make interdisciplinary connections through assignments, activities, and/or experiences.

INTERDISCIPLINARY: Provide an abbreviated reading list organized by discipline that demonstrates the course’s disciplinary perspectives, and explain how each disciplinary perspective is integrated into major course assignments and activities.
ETHICS: Identify the ethical framework that allows students to weigh/evaluate issues. This topic needs to show up explicitly in the course schedule.
ETHICS: List the readings pertaining to ethics.
ETHICS: Describe how ethics is incorporated in some/all of the assignments and activities.
# Submit to the Workflow
Once you have finalized your proposal draft:
Select Leave Edit Mode in the upper-right corner of the screen, just below the orange bar.
Select Submit for Approval to submit the proposal to the workflow.
# So, what happens now?

Your proposal will automatically be sent to the appropriate review committees. You may be contacted within Kuali Comments by the committees with questions to the proposal (an email will notify you automatically). You can also return to your proposal from your dashboard at any time to view the workflow status.

Requisites

Requisites are courses, conditions, or other requirements that determine whether a student is eligible to enroll in a course. Requisites may be required before enrollment, at the time of enrollment, or may establish other conditions for registration.
Common types of requisites include:
Prerequisites: Courses or requirements that must be completed before enrolling in the course.
Corequisites: Courses or requirements that must be completed concurrently with the course.
Other enrollment requirements: Additional conditions that may apply to enrollment, such as minimum class standing, program or major restrictions, or other eligibility requirements.
When entering requisites in Kuali, ensure that the requirements accurately reflect the conditions under which students should be permitted to enroll.

lines: Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "class component.”
Method of Instruction

Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.
# Lecture
A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
# Laboratory
Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
# Recitation
Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
# Studio
Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
# Seminar
Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
# Independent Study

One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
# Practicum
Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
# Workshop
Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.

If a program is currently offered on the Traditional Academic Calendar and you would like to move it to the Accelerated Academic Calendar, you cannot simply change the calendar while students are still enrolled in the program. The existing program must first be fully taught out. This requires a proposal to suspend admission to the program. Once there are no students remaining in the program, the program can be moved from one academic calendar to the other.

Alternatively, you may propose a new program by cloning the existing program. This approach does not require Board of Trustees approval and is treated as a program modification. Proposal Development
Faculty use the forms in Kuali Curriculum Management to develop the proposal and work with other stakeholders as appropriate.

Department Review
The proposal is reviewed through the appropriate departmental process.

College Curriculum Committee Review
The College Curriculum Committee reviews the proposal.

College Dean Approval
The College Dean approves the proposal for Faculty Senate review.

Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee Review
The Curriculum & Standards Committee, the General Education Committee, or the Graduate Council reviews the proposal.

Faculty Senate Approval
The Faculty Senate considers the curriculum committee's recommendation and votes.

University President Approval
Any curricular item that is not a course must be reviewed and approved by the University President.

URI Board of Trustees Approval
In addition to the University President’s approval, new Majors and Degrees are also reviewed by the Board of Trustees.
# Workflows by College / Academic Group

While all Colleges follow the curriculum approval process established in the University Manual, each College may have its own internal approval process based on its departmental and governance structures. To download a flowchart of a specific College’s approval process, select the College below.
# Workflow Process Common Questions
# Do I have to obtain a Library Impact Statement before submitting a proposal?

No, the Library Impact Statement is completed within the Kuali proposal for all new courses, degrees, and majors, and is automatically routed to the Library Subject Selector to review and attach the LIS to the form.
# Do I have to meet with the Learning Outcomes & Oversight Committee regarding my Assessment Plan prior to submitting my new degree, major, or certificate proposal?

No, you simply need to complete the appropriate assessment plan and attach it to the proposal. Once the proposal is submitted to the workflow, a notification is sent to the Associate Director of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation, and members from the team will be in touch if any follow-up or revisions are necessary.

Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.

Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

Specialization Description

The University Catalog description of the requirements for completing a specialization within an academic program, including the specialization-specific courses and credits required in addition to the program’s core requirements, as well as any additional specialization-specific requirements.
# Description Formatting for the Catalog/Kuali
# Specialization Description Formatting
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose and significance of the specialization.
Course Requirements
Important: Do not include program requirements in the specialization description.
Only include the requirements of the specialization in the specialization description, and exclude the core requirements to the program. The specialization

A specialization is an addition to the academic program, not a second listing of the program’s requirements. Students complete the requirements of the program and, where applicable, the additional requirements of their chosen specialization. The specialization description should therefore include only the requirements that are specific to that specialization.

Repeating the program requirements within the specialization could imply that students must complete those requirements again as part of the specialization. Keeping program-wide requirements in the program description and specialization-specific requirements in the specialization description makes it clear which requirements apply to the program as a whole and which are additional requirements for the specialization.
(For ABMs only) Courses that are able to be double-counted

# Specialization Requirements
A minimum GPA average of 2.00 must be earned in the specialization courses (UM 8.20.61)
Half of the credits required for the specialization must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.61)
A maximum of one third of the total credits required for a master’s program may be double counted for an ABM program. (UM 8.30.19)

pages.title: Kuali Basics
lines: Kuali Basics
Quick Links
# What is Kuali Curriculum Management?

Kuali Curriculum Management (CM) is URI’s system for managing university curriculum and the curriculum approval process. It uses electronic forms and workflow to route course, program, and specialization proposals through the appropriate levels of review and approval.
# Kuali, the Catalog, and eCampus
Kuali serves as the central source for approved curriculum information:
Kuali CM — Manages curriculum proposals and the approval workflow.
Academic Catalog — Pulls approved course, program, and specialization information from Kuali.
eCampus — Receives approved course information from Kuali for implementation in future terms.
# Why it matters

Information entered into Kuali can flow directly into the official academic catalog and eCampus. Proposals should therefore be clear, accurate, and unambiguous, as the information entered during the proposal process becomes part of the University’s official curriculum.
# Access & Logging Into Kuali
Access to Kuali CM is limited to faculty, Deans, and select administrators and staff. Only faculty members may submit curriculum proposals.
# Faculty Access

Faculty members automatically have access to Kuali CM, as faculty are the users authorized to submit curricular proposals. If this is your first time accessing Kuali CM, sign in using your URI Microsoft 365 account.
# Non-Faculty Access
Access to Kuali CM is also available to deans and select administrators or staff. In specific cases, other non-faculty users may request access.

Use the Kuali Access Package to request access using your URI SSO. After selecting Continue, you will be asked to provide your job or position title and a business justification for needing access. Once your request has been reviewed, you will be notified whether access has been granted.
# Logging In
Sign in to your Microsoft 365 Apps using your URI SSO.
Select Kuali Course Management from your application collection.
Alternatively, use the direct link to Kuali CM and bookmark it for future access.
# Accessing the Curriculum App
Once logged in, select the Curriculum tile. This is where you can view current courses, programs, and specializations and, for authorized users, create proposals for new or modified curriculum.
# The Kuali Dashboard
When you enter Curriculum Management, the Dashboard serves as your homepage. It provides quick access to your proposals and items requiring your action.
# My Proposals
My Proposals allows you to:
Continue working on Drafts you have started but not yet submitted.
View submitted proposals and their current workflow status.
Access proposals directly from the Dashboard.
Any proposals you begin but have not yet submitted will appear as Drafts. From this section, you can continue editing or delete a draft.
Select View All to see your complete list of proposals. The list can be filtered, downloaded, and printed.
# My Action List
My Action List displays your ten most recent items requiring action. These may include proposals that require you to:
Review and approve
Acknowledge
Edit and return to the workflow after being sent back by a reviewing committee
# Navigating Kuali
Use the navigation bar on the left side of the screen to access courses, programs, specializations, and proposals, including drafts, proposals under review, and approved records.
# 🔎 Search and Filters
Use the search bar at the top of the Courses, Programs, Specializations, or Proposals pages to locate specific records. Use the filters on the right side of the page to narrow your results.
Status: Select Active when searching for current curricular items. Retired and Inactive statuses are not consistently used in Kuali CM.
Groups: Use Groups to locate curricular records associated with a specific department or college.
# Versioning
Kuali uses colored bars to indicate which version of a curricular record you are viewing.

🟢 Current Version — The version currently in effect. For most records, the earliest version available in Kuali is Fall 2022, when URI began using Kuali. Earlier historical versions are available in eCampus.
⚪ Past Version — An earlier version of the record, including inactive records.
🟣 Future Version — A version scheduled to become active in a future term.
↕️ Use the arrows next to the term dates to expand the record history and select an earlier or future version.
# Proposal Status

The status indicators below apply only when you are viewing a proposal and not the curricular record itself. The colored bar at the top of a proposal indicates where the proposal is in the curriculum approval workflow.
🟡 Draft — A new proposal or proposed change that has been created but not yet submitted to the workflow. Drafts can be edited or deleted.
🔵 Under Review — A proposal that has been submitted to the workflow and is currently moving through the approval process.
⚫ Denied — A proposal that has been denied during the review process. Denied proposals cannot be edited or resubmitted.
🟢 Approved — A proposal that has completed the required approval process and has been approved.
Tip: When viewing an approved proposal, you can switch to the current curricular record by selecting “View Active Course (Program / Specialization).”

New Temporary & Permanent Course Email

The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:

Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.

Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

Short Description: Student-facing summary of a course that clearly and concisely communicates its content, purpose, and focus.
Course Description

Course descriptions are written for students, not faculty, and must communicate clearly and concisely to them. Jargon, acronyms, and technical language should be avoided as much as possible. Anyone should be able to read the description and understand the nature and intent of the course.

An acceptable course description with a maximum of 30 words, begins with a verb, e.g. examines, introduces, explores, investigates. Articles, adjectives and adverbs are seldom necessary. Sentence fragments are acceptable.

Short Description: Identifies how a curricular offering is delivered, including in-person, online, or a combination of in-person and online instruction.
Modality

Modality identifies the method of delivery for a curricular offering, including courses, programs, and specializations. It describes whether instruction occurs in person, online, or through a combination of in-person and online instruction.
The University recognizes the following modalities:
# In-Person Modalities
In Person
Instruction occurs at a specified physical location on specified days and times. Less than 25% of instruction is delivered online.
In Person & Online Asynchronous

Instruction combines in-person meetings on specified days and times with online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus on the first day of class. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
In Person & Online Synchronous
Instruction combines in-person and online meetings on specified days and times. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
# Online Modalities
Online Synchronous
All instruction occurs online at specified days and times.
Online Synchronous & Asynchronous

All instruction occurs online and combines synchronous meetings on specified days and times with asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
Online Asynchronous

All instruction occurs online with no required synchronous meetings at specified days and times, except for optional online office hours or meetings. The weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus.
See University Manual 8.30.30
